sec-desc: Vault data is encrypted on-device. Protection depends on master-password strength, the KDF parameters stored with the vault, device security, and how the application is used. No cryptographic design guarantees protection in every attack scenario.
sec-c1-desc: Every record is encrypted using an isolated 256-bit AES-GCM key derived via WebCrypto HKDF-SHA256 per item.
sec-c2-desc: Argon2id raises the cost of offline password guessing. Defaults: Tauri native desktop/Android, 64 MiB / 4 iterations / 2 lanes; Web/WASM, 32 MiB / 3 iterations / 1 lane. Existing vaults keep their stored parameters.
sec-c3-desc: The master password and derived keys are processed client-side. Protection also depends on the security of the device running the application and the user's environment.

flow-s1-desc: Master password is entered and immediately converted to a secure Uint8Array buffer.
flow-s2-desc: Tauri native desktop/Android: 64 MiB / 4 passes / 2 lanes. Web/WASM: 32 MiB / 3 passes / 1 lane.
flow-s3-desc: KEK decrypts the isolated Database Encryption Key (DEK) via AES-256-GCM.
flow-s4-desc: Decrypted DEK interacts with SQLite inside Origin Private File System via WebCrypto.
flow-s5-desc: On vault lock or timeout, all cryptographic keys are securely zeroized from RAM.
feat-desc: An architecture designed for frictionless productivity without lowering security boundaries.
feat-c1-desc: Your credentials live in your browser or desktop app's isolated Origin Private File System directly inside a native SQLite database. 100% resilient to network outages.
feat-c2-desc: The desktop application communicates with the extension over a dynamically selected loopback TCP port. A pairing token authenticates the connection, and XChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypts message frames.
feat-c3-desc: The network policy restricts unexpected outbound connections. Offline use is supported; enabled features and configuration can affect network behavior.
feat-c4-desc: Generate and autofill RFC 6238 time-based one-time codes without relying on external 2FA mobile apps.
feat-c5-desc: Unlock your vault effortlessly using Windows Hello, Touch ID, Face ID, or Android Biometrics through native platform bindings.

p-password-vault-h1: One vault for every kind of credential
p-password-vault-lead: Five record types, folders, tags, smart folders and full-text search — all encrypted on your device, all readable offline.
p-password-vault-what-title: A vault that does not need a server
p-password-vault-p1: The vault stores five kinds of record: logins, payment cards, identities, secure keys and secure notes. Every record is encrypted with its own key, so one record being broken never reveals another.
p-password-vault-p2: Organisation is local too. Folders, tags, favourites and built-in smart folders such as "has 2FA" or "missing 2FA" are computed on the device from your own data, not from a server-side index.
p-password-vault-p3: Search runs locally across titles, usernames and URLs, with diacritic-insensitive matching, so it keeps working with no connection at all.
p-password-vault-step1-desc: Argon2id stretches it into a key. The parameters are recorded in the vault, so an existing vault never silently gets weaker or stronger.
p-password-vault-step2-title: Each record gets its own key
p-password-vault-step2-desc: A unique 256-bit AES-256-GCM key is derived per record through WebCrypto HKDF-SHA256, using the record id as the salt.
p-password-vault-step3-desc: Titles, usernames, passwords and notes are masked in the SQLite columns; the real values exist only inside the encrypted payload.
p-password-vault-shot-desc: Logins, cards, secure keys, identities and notes share one editor, and a payment card keeps its number, expiry, CVV and ATM PIN in separate masked fields.
p-password-vault-sec-title: What the encryption does and does not promise
p-password-vault-sec-label: Read this before you trust it with your vault
p-password-vault-sec-body: Every record is encrypted on your device with a key that never leaves it. Protection still depends on your master password strength, the KDF parameters stored in your vault, the security of the device itself, and how you use the application. No cryptographic design promises absolute protection against every attack, and a compromised device can read a vault that has already been unlocked.
p-password-vault-tech1-desc: New desktop and Android vaults use 64 MiB of memory, 4 iterations and 2 lanes. Web builds use 32 MiB, 3 iterations and 1 lane.
p-password-vault-tech2-desc: Breaking one record does not reveal any other record in the vault, because no two records share a key.
p-password-vault-tech3-desc: Sensitive columns hold a static placeholder token. The plaintext exists only inside the AES-256-GCM payload.
p-password-vault-faq1-q: What happens if I forget my master password?
p-password-vault-faq1-a: You can unlock with the 24-word BIP-39 recovery key and reset the password, or restore an encrypted backup. Without either, the vault cannot be opened, because nothing on your device can re-derive the key.
p-password-vault-faq2-q: Can I open the same vault on another computer?
p-password-vault-faq2-a: Yes. Export an encrypted backup and restore it on the other device with your master password. The vault file is portable and not tied to one machine.
p-password-vault-faq3-q: Does search send anything to a server?
p-password-vault-faq3-a: No. Search runs against the local database on your device, including diacritic-insensitive matching.
p-passkeys-h1: Passkeys that never leave your vault
p-passkeys-lead: Create WebAuthn credentials inside your own vault, bound to the authenticator your device already has. Nothing is registered with a third party.
p-passkeys-p1: A passkey is created through the WebAuthn API of your platform, so the private half of the credential never enters the vault in a usable form and never leaves your device. The vault stores the credential id and its metadata so you can recognise and revoke it later.
p-passkeys-p2: The page reports which authenticator is available before you create anything, and lets you choose the relying party, display name, account and signature algorithm.
p-passkeys-p3: Passkeys sit alongside the rest of the vault rather than in a separate system, so they are encrypted, searchable and restorable in exactly the same way as a password.
p-passkeys-step1-title: Your device creates the key pair
p-passkeys-step1-desc: The private key is generated inside the platform authenticator — TPM 2.0, Secure Enclave or AndroidKeyStore — and is not exportable.
p-passkeys-step2-desc: Only the credential id and display metadata are saved, encrypted with the rest of the vault.
p-passkeys-step3-desc: Because the private key is non-exportable, a signature for a site cannot be produced by anything other than the authenticator itself.
p-passkeys-shot-title: Hardware unlock sits next to it
p-passkeys-shot-desc: The same settings panel holds the FIDO2 and biometric unlock options, so passkeys and hardware-bound unlocking live together rather than in separate products.
p-passkeys-sec-title: What passkeys do and do not remove
p-passkeys-sec-label: Passkeys are not a backup plan
p-passkeys-sec-body: A passkey replaces the password at a site; it does not replace your vault. If you lose the device holding your authenticator and have no passkey stored elsewhere, that credential is gone with it. Passkeys also only help at sites that support WebAuthn, which is most large services and a growing share of smaller ones.
p-passkeys-tech1-desc: Credentials are created through the WebAuthn API, so they are the same kind of object any compliant site expects.
p-passkeys-tech2-desc: Hardware-backed authenticators generate the key pair and never release the private half, so copying your vault does not copy the credential.
p-passkeys-tech3-desc: Credential records are encrypted by the same per-item key scheme as the rest of your vault.
p-passkeys-faq1-q: Do I still need my master password?
p-passkeys-faq1-a: Yes. The vault itself is unlocked by your master password and secret key. A passkey only replaces the password at the specific sites where you register one.
p-passkeys-faq2-a: Any platform authenticator your device exposes: Windows Hello, Touch ID, Face ID, Android biometrics, or a FIDO2 security key such as YubiKey.
p-passkeys-faq3-q: What if I lose the device?
p-passkeys-faq3-a: That specific passkey is lost with its authenticator. Your vault, its passwords and its backups are unaffected, because those never depended on that device.
p-vault-history-h1: Mistakes are reversible, on your own schedule
p-vault-history-lead: Deleted records stay recoverable for 15 days, every item keeps its own password history, and encrypted snapshots let you travel back without asking anyone.
p-vault-history-what-title: Three separate ways to undo a mistake
p-vault-history-p1: Deletion is not destruction. Removing an entry moves it into an encrypted local trash that is cleaned automatically after fifteen days, and you can restore it or purge it at any point inside that window.
p-vault-history-p2: Every item keeps its own password history, so you can see what a password used to be and roll it back when it turns out to have been rotated somewhere you forgot about.
p-vault-history-p3: Snapshots are versioned: the app can take one on demand or automatically on a schedule you choose, encrypts each before writing, and prunes the oldest once your retention limit is reached.
p-vault-history-step1-desc: A snapshot records the current state of your vault, either when you press the button or on the schedule you configured.
p-vault-history-step2-desc: Each snapshot is encrypted on device before it is written to storage, so a snapshot file is never readable on its own.
p-vault-history-step3-desc: Once the retention limit is reached the oldest snapshots are removed, so the local history cannot grow without bound.
p-vault-history-shot-desc: The trash explains its own behaviour in the product: deleted records stay on your device and can be restored or permanently removed at any time inside the window.
p-vault-history-sec-title: Where backups are stored, and who holds the key
p-vault-history-sec-body: Local snapshots and exported backups are encrypted with Argon2id and AES-256-GCM, and the password for an exported backup can be your master password. Optional cloud sync is off by default; if you enable it against your own WebDAV or S3 storage, your vault is encrypted on the device before it is sent, so the provider only ever receives ciphertext. That convenience depends on your storage account staying reachable — the vault file itself remains portable and restorable without it.
p-vault-history-tech1-desc: A snapshot or exported backup is encrypted on device, so the file is useless on its own without your password.
p-vault-history-tech2-desc: Sync providers receive ciphertext only. Nobody but you can decrypt what you store there.
p-vault-history-tech3-desc: Bitwarden, LastPass, 1Password, Chrome CSV and JSON exports are processed entirely on your device.
p-vault-history-faq1-q: Is a deleted record really gone?
p-vault-history-faq1-a: Not for fifteen days. It sits in an encrypted local trash that you can restore from or purge early.
p-vault-history-faq2-a: No. Snapshots, encrypted exports and restores all work on a single device with no account and no network.
p-vault-history-faq3-q: Can I move my vault to another manager later?
p-vault-history-faq3-a: Nothing prevents it, but note that exports are your choice: use the encrypted backup format rather than a plaintext JSON dump if you want the file to stay protected.
p-security-audit-h1: Find the passwords that are actually costing you
p-security-audit-lead: The audit scores your vault and separates each problem: short passwords, passwords shared between accounts, passwords in known breach data, accounts with no second factor, plain HTTP links and records nobody has touched in a year.
p-security-audit-what-title: An audit that runs where your data already is
p-security-audit-p1: Most password audits tell you a score and stop. This one splits the score into the individual problems that caused it, because "your vault is weak" is not actionable while "this one account has no second factor" is.
p-security-audit-p2: Weak, reused and breached are tracked separately. The breach check runs against the k-anonymity style range queries used by Have I Been Pwned, so it can compare your passwords against a known corpus without sending the passwords themselves anywhere.
p-security-audit-p3: The same categories are available as built-in smart folders, so you can jump straight from a finding to the item that caused it instead of hunting through the list.
p-security-audit-step1-desc: The vault is decrypted in memory on your device and each item is scored. Nothing about the audit is transmitted.
p-security-audit-step2-desc: Weak, reused, breached, missing second factor, insecure transport and outdated are counted independently rather than folded into one number.
p-security-audit-step3-desc: Each finding links to the record that produced it, so a fix is one click away rather than a manual search.
p-security-audit-shot-title: Fixing a finding is one step away
p-security-audit-shot-desc: The built-in generator produces a replacement with the character classes you choose, so a weak password can be replaced without leaving the audit flow.
p-security-audit-sec-title: What the audit can and cannot tell you
p-security-audit-sec-label: A score is not a guarantee
p-security-audit-sec-body: The audit measures your vault against known heuristics and known breach corpora. It cannot tell you whether a password you still use was exposed somewhere that has never published a dataset, whether a strong password is reused somewhere it could not check, or whether an account you saved is still yours to access. It reports what it can see in your own data, and nothing more.
p-security-audit-tech1-desc: Passwords are compared using range queries so only a hash prefix leaves the device, and the passwords themselves never do.
p-security-audit-tech2-desc: Scoring happens against your decrypted vault on the device, so the audit works with no connection at all.
p-security-audit-tech3-desc: Weak, reused, breached, missing 2FA, insecure HTTP and outdated records are counted independently.
p-security-audit-faq1-q: Does the audit send my passwords anywhere?
p-security-audit-faq1-a: No. The scoring runs locally. The breach comparison uses range queries, so only a hash prefix is involved and the password itself never leaves the device.
p-security-audit-faq2-q: How often should I run it?
p-security-audit-faq2-a: Whenever you add or change records, and after adding a large import from another manager. A large import is the most common reason a strong vault suddenly scores badly.
p-security-audit-faq3-q: Does a low score mean I was hacked?
p-security-audit-faq3-a: No. The score describes the passwords in your vault, not whether any of them have been exposed. It measures what is recoverable from your own data.
p-password-generator-h1: Two ways to make a password you will not have to remember
p-password-generator-lead: Generate a random-character password from the classes you pick, or roll a Diceware phrase you can actually recall. Strength is measured on your device as it is produced.
p-password-generator-what-title: Randomness you can inspect instead of trusting
p-password-generator-p1: The character mode lets you choose the length and which classes are in play — upper case, lower case, digits, symbols — and shows the strength of the result before you accept it. If you leave a class out, that is a weaker password, and the strength bar says so rather than quietly overriding you.
p-password-generator-p2: The Diceware mode produces a phrase from a word list instead. Longer, easier to spell and to remember, and usually stronger per character than a short random string.
p-password-generator-p3: Whatever you generate is a normal vault record: it is encrypted on save, masked until you ask to see it, and can be copied straight to the clipboard with a timed clear.
p-password-generator-step1-desc: Values are drawn from the platform cryptographic random source rather than a seeded generator, so the result is not reproducible from anything you can observe.
p-password-generator-step2-desc: The estimate is computed on your device and shown next to the result; no part of the password is sent anywhere to be measured.
p-password-generator-step3-title: Saving encrypts it like any record
p-password-generator-step3-desc: Once you accept a password it becomes a normal vault record and is encrypted with that item's own key.
p-password-generator-shot-title: Check the result before you keep it
p-password-generator-shot-desc: The audit scores what you generate the same way it scores everything else, so a new password can be verified in the same place it will be stored.
p-password-generator-sec-label: A strong password on a reused site is still a reused password
p-password-generator-sec-body: Generating a strong password protects that credential only if the site stores it well and you use it nowhere else. It does not protect a password that was reused across several services before you generated a new one, and it does not defend a session that is already being intercepted. Pair the generator with passkeys where a site supports them, and with the security audit to find what needs replacing.
p-password-generator-tech1-desc: Random values come from the platform cryptographic source, not from a seeded pseudo-random generator.
p-password-generator-tech2-desc: A phrase from a word list is usually stronger per character and far easier to recall than a random string.
p-password-generator-tech3-desc: Copied values are cleared from the clipboard on a timer, so a password does not sit in the clipboard indefinitely.
p-password-generator-faq1-q: How long should a generated password be?
p-password-generator-faq1-a: Length matters more than symbol soup. Sixteen characters or more is a reasonable floor, and a Diceware phrase of five or six words is comparable or better while being easier to type.
p-password-generator-faq2-q: Does it remember my generator settings?
p-password-generator-faq2-a: The generator reflects the choices you make in the panel; it does not silently add character classes you switched off.
p-password-generator-faq3-q: Can I use the generator offline?
p-password-generator-faq3-a: Yes. It is a local feature and needs no connection.
p-unlock-and-recovery-h1: Convenient unlock, without giving up recovery
p-unlock-and-recovery-lead: Biometrics and hardware keys can stand in for the master password. They only remove friction: the vault key still derives from master password plus secret key, and a 24-word recovery kit stays available.
p-unlock-and-recovery-what-title: Two independent ways back into the vault
p-unlock-and-recovery-p1: Unlock can be delegated to the hardware you already carry. Windows Hello, Touch ID, Face ID, Android biometrics or a FIDO2 key such as YubiKey can satisfy the authentication step, so you do not type a long master password every morning.
p-unlock-and-recovery-p2: Recovery is a separate path entirely. A 24-word BIP-39 recovery phrase can unlock and reset the vault if the master password and the device are both gone, and the emergency kit that carries it is written to a file you control rather than to a vendor.
p-unlock-and-recovery-p3: A password hint exists for the in-between case, stored in plaintext on purpose so it can actually remind you — which is why the product warns you not to put the password itself in it.
p-unlock-and-recovery-step1-title: The authenticator wraps the vault key
p-unlock-and-recovery-step1-desc: Inside a non-exportable keystore, PBKDF2-SHA256 and AES-GCM wrap the vault key so that unlocking can be authorised by the platform authenticator.
p-unlock-and-recovery-step2-desc: Vault access always derives from master password plus secret key through Argon2id. Hardware binding is a layer on top, never the foundation.
p-unlock-and-recovery-step3-title: Losing the authenticator costs convenience only
p-unlock-and-recovery-step3-desc: A lost or replaced authenticator does not affect the vault file, its backups, or any record inside it.
p-unlock-and-recovery-shot-title: Where all three secrets are chosen
p-unlock-and-recovery-shot-desc: Master password, account secret key and the emergency kit are collected once, at setup, on your own device — there is no server-side account to recover them from.
p-unlock-and-recovery-sec-title: Where convenience ends and risk begins
p-unlock-and-recovery-sec-label: A hint is a hint, not a backup
p-unlock-and-recovery-sec-body: Hardware unlock means anyone who can authenticate on the device, or who holds your security key, can open the vault — that is the point, and it is why device and key security matter. The password hint is stored in plaintext precisely so it can be read back to you, so it must never contain the password itself. A recovery phrase should be written down and kept offline: anyone who reads it can reset your vault.
p-unlock-and-recovery-tech1-desc: The platform authenticator is TPM-backed on Windows, and the wrapping key material does not leave that boundary.
p-unlock-and-recovery-tech2-desc: On macOS the platform authenticator output is sealed by the Secure Enclave.
p-unlock-and-recovery-tech3-desc: A 24-word recovery phrase can unlock and reset the vault when the password and the device are both unavailable.
p-unlock-and-recovery-faq1-q: Does enabling hardware unlock weaken the vault?
p-unlock-and-recovery-faq1-a: It changes who can open the vault, not how it is encrypted. The records stay encrypted with the same keys, and access still derives from your master password and secret key.
p-unlock-and-recovery-faq2-q: What happens if I lose my security key?
p-unlock-and-recovery-faq2-a: You fall back to the master password, and if you have lost that too, the recovery kit. The vault itself is unaffected — only the convenience factor is gone.
p-unlock-and-recovery-faq3-q: Where should I keep the recovery kit?
p-unlock-and-recovery-faq3-a: Offline, physically, somewhere you would still find it in several years. It is a master key: whoever reads it can reset your vault.
p-autofill-h1: One click, and only on the site you meant
p-autofill-lead: The extension matches by registrable domain, not by URL string, so a shared host never receives the wrong credential. The dropdown renders inside a closed Shadow DOM the page cannot reach.
p-autofill-what-title: Matching that cannot be fooled by a lookalike host
p-autofill-p1: A URL is reduced to its registrable domain using the full Mozilla Public Suffix List, embedded in the extension as a hash-pinned snapshot. Hostnames are never compared as raw strings, so a subdomain cannot borrow a credential that belongs to a different site.
p-autofill-p2: The dropdown, the password generator and the phishing warning all render inside a closed Shadow DOM attached to the page. The page's own JavaScript cannot read them, rewrite them, or overlay them to capture what you type.
p-autofill-p3: The extension talks to the desktop app over a dynamic loopback port, and message frames are encrypted. Copying a password puts it on the clipboard on a timer, so it does not sit there indefinitely.
p-autofill-step1-desc: The content script notices a login field and asks the app for the credentials that belong to this site.
p-autofill-step2-desc: Your URL is normalised to eTLD+1 with the embedded Public Suffix List, then matched against the vault's stored domains.
p-autofill-step3-desc: The dropdown shows only the records for that domain, and the chosen one is typed into the field.
p-autofill-shot-title: The same app, on desktop and mobile
p-autofill-shot-desc: The extension is one front end to the same local vault, so a credential you add on the desktop is available to the browser immediately.
p-autofill-sec-title: What autofill does not protect you from
p-autofill-sec-label: Autofill is convenience, not a control
p-autofill-sec-body: Autofill fills a form; it does not decide whether the site is honest. The extension checks for obvious phishing by comparing the domain against what your vault already knows, but a site that impersonates a domain you have never saved will look new rather than familiar. A password manager reduces typing errors and reuse. It does not replace two-factor authentication, and it cannot help once credentials have already been entered into a page that was hostile all along.
p-autofill-tech1-desc: Built on the full Mozilla Public Suffix List as a hash-pinned snapshot, so shared hosting is handled correctly.
p-autofill-tech2-desc: Dropdown, generator and phishing warning render where the page's own script cannot see or modify them.
p-autofill-tech3-desc: Content scripts match http and https only, so internal browser schemes are out of scope.
p-autofill-faq1-q: Does the extension need an internet connection?
p-autofill-faq1-a: No. Everything it needs is on your device: the vault is local, and the connection to the desktop app is a loopback port on your own machine.
p-autofill-faq2-q: What happens if the desktop app is closed?
p-autofill-faq2-a: The popup says the vault is locked and the dropdown reports no records. Nothing is cached in the browser, so a closed app means no autofill.
p-autofill-faq3-a: Chrome, Edge and Firefox, using Manifest V3. A Safari build exists and needs a local wrapper to run it.
p-attachments-h1: Keep the file with the credential, not in a downloads folder
p-attachments-lead: Recovery codes, identity documents, certificates and warranty files attach to the record they belong to, and they are encrypted with that record rather than sitting in a plain downloads folder.
p-attachments-what-title: Files treated like credentials, not like downloads
p-attachments-p1: An attachment belongs to a record. Delete the record and the file goes with it, and restore the record and the file comes back with it. It is stored the way the record is stored, not as a loose file somewhere in your profile.
p-attachments-p2: The file is encrypted on your device before it is written. A single record can hold up to 250 MB, so a scanned ID, a certificate bundle or a short video fits inside the encrypted database rather than in plaintext on disk.
p-attachments-p3: Attachments follow the record when you export an encrypted backup, which means a full restore on another device brings the files along with the credentials.
p-attachments-step1-desc: Drag a file into the record, or pick one. The size limit is 250 MB per file.
p-attachments-step2-desc: The content is encrypted on the device using the same scheme as the record it belongs to.
p-attachments-step3-desc: Only ciphertext is written to the encrypted IndexedDB; nothing readable is left behind on disk.
p-attachments-shot-title: The record the file belongs to
p-attachments-shot-desc: Payment cards keep their number, expiry, CVV and ATM PIN in separate masked fields, with the file attached alongside them under one encrypted record.
p-attachments-sec-label: Encryption is not a smaller attack surface
p-attachments-sec-body: An attachment is encrypted at rest like the rest of your vault, so a stolen device file does not hand over your documents. It does not change the rest of the model: a weak master password, a compromised device or a vault you have already unlocked still exposes what is inside. Attachments make a record larger and more valuable, not safer than the record itself. Treat a vault holding identity documents as more sensitive than one holding only passwords.
p-attachments-tech1-desc: Enough for a scanned document, a certificate bundle or a short clip without leaving encrypted storage.
p-attachments-tech2-desc: Files land in an encrypted IndexedDB rather than the plain filesystem.
p-attachments-tech3-desc: Attachments are included in an encrypted backup and restored together with the credential.
p-attachments-faq1-a: The editor accepts the common document, image, video and archive types and encrypts whatever it accepts. A single file is limited to 250 MB.
p-attachments-faq2-q: Can I open an attachment from another device?
p-attachments-faq2-a: Yes, after restoring the encrypted backup. The file travels with the record rather than as a separate download.
p-attachments-faq3-q: What happens to attachments when I delete a record?
p-attachments-faq3-a: They follow the record into the encrypted trash for the same 15 day window, and are removed with it if you delete permanently.
p-guvenlik-h1: Security that starts on your device
p-guvenlik-lead: KalderaShield is a local-first password manager: your vault lives on your device, encryption happens there, and no account or cloud copy is required. This section explains exactly how that protection works — and where it ends.
p-guvenlik-what-title: A vault that has no server to breach
p-guvenlik-p1: There is no KalderaShield account and no server-side vault copy. Your encrypted vault is stored on your device and, if you choose, in encrypted backup files that you move yourself. An attacker cannot breach a server that does not exist.
p-guvenlik-p2: Every record is encrypted separately. A unique 256-bit AES-256-GCM key is derived per record through HKDF-SHA256, so decrypting one item never exposes another. Titles, usernames, passwords and notes exist in plaintext only inside the authenticated ciphertext payload.
p-guvenlik-p3: The master password is stretched with Argon2id — 64 MiB of memory, 4 iterations and 2 lanes on desktop and Android — and the parameters are stored in the vault, so an existing vault never silently becomes weaker.
p-guvenlik-p4: Production builds run behind an air-gap policy: unexpected outbound fetch, WebSocket, WebRTC and similar calls are blocked and logged. The only network traffic is the Have I Been Pwned range check, which sends the first five characters of a SHA-1 hash and never your password.
p-guvenlik-step1-title: Your master password is the root
p-guvenlik-step1-desc: Argon2id turns it into the vault key. The master password is never stored in browser sessionStorage; after unlock, session state is a zeroized in-memory byte buffer, not a string the page can read.
p-guvenlik-step2-desc: Windows Hello (TPM 2.0), macOS Touch ID (Secure Enclave), Android BiometricPrompt (AndroidKeyStore) and PRF-capable FIDO2 keys wrap the unlock payload. The vault file itself is never hardware-sealed, so a lost device never locks you out.
p-guvenlik-step3-desc: The published threat model states which attacks are defended, which are only partially defended, and which are out of scope — including malware running in your own OS session. Product claims are not allowed to promise more.
p-guvenlik-sec-title: What this protection does not cover
p-guvenlik-sec-body: No local application can protect a vault on a compromised device: malware running with your OS account while the vault is unlocked, keyloggers, privileged screen capture and memory inspection are all outside this model. Hardware unlock is a convenience wrapper, not a replacement for the master password. An independent third-party audit has not been completed yet — that is stated openly, not hidden.
p-guvenlik-tech1-desc: 64 MiB, 4 iterations, 2 lanes for new desktop and Android vaults; 32 MiB, 3 iterations, 1 lane for web builds.
p-guvenlik-tech2-desc: HKDF-SHA256 derives a unique key per record and per attachment, with the record id as salt. Tampered ciphertext fails authentication.
p-guvenlik-tech3-desc: Unexpected outbound fetch, XHR, WebSocket, sendBeacon, EventSource and WebRTC destinations are blocked and recorded as security events.
p-guvenlik-faq1-q: Is my vault ever sent to a server?
p-guvenlik-faq1-a: No. There is no account and no server-side vault. Optional sync providers such as WebDAV and S3 upload only the encrypted payload to storage that you configure and own.
p-guvenlik-faq2-q: Can KalderaShield recover my master password?
p-guvenlik-faq2-a: No, and no one else can either. Unlock with the master password, unlock with the 24-word BIP-39 recovery key, or restore an encrypted backup. Without one of those, the vault cannot be opened.
p-guvenlik-faq3-q: Has an independent audit been performed?
p-guvenlik-faq3-a: Not yet. The audit status page states this openly and describes the automated verification that is in place today. Hiding an unfinished audit would contradict everything else on this site.
p-tehdit-modeli-h1: What we defend against — and what we do not
p-tehdit-modeli-lead: A password manager that claims to stop every attack is lying to you. This page is the public summary of the desktop threat model: the attacks the design defends against, the ones it only partially defends against, and the ones it deliberately does not.
p-tehdit-modeli-p1: The model covers the desktop application running as a local vault: master password setup, unlock, lock and reset; persistence in the wa-sqlite backend and legacy OPFS/JSON stores awaiting guarded migration; encrypted backups; attachment encryption; biometric convenience unlock; and clipboard and revealed-field behaviour while the app is unlocked.
p-tehdit-modeli-p2: Protected assets include the master password, every vault item secret — passwords, cards, API keys, passkey records, identities, notes, TOTP seeds and ownership-revealing metadata — attachment contents, encrypted backup files and the biometric-wrapped unlock payload.
p-tehdit-modeli-p3: Trust boundaries are explicit. Browser-like storage APIs count as persistence, not secret storage. OPFS and localStorage fallbacks are treated as attacker-readable at rest unless the app encrypted them. Imported CSV/JSON data and user-selected backup files are untrusted input until parsed and validated.
p-tehdit-modeli-step1-desc: A copied encrypted .ks backup without its password. Reading the persisted database payload while locked. Tampering with AES-GCM backup or attachment payloads. Malformed import files. Brief physical access after the app has locked.
p-tehdit-modeli-step2-desc: A process with your OS user account reading application storage: item payloads and attachments are encrypted, but profile settings and some metadata may remain readable. A valid unlocked session: auto-lock and reveal reset reduce exposure, but unlocked is still trusted.
p-tehdit-modeli-step3-desc: Malware running as your OS user while the vault is unlocked. A compromised OS, WebView or runtime. Memory inspection, keylogging, privileged screen capture and clipboard capture by hostile local software. Losing the master password with no valid backup. Cloud sync, multi-device conflict resolution and enterprise policy are not shipped features and are outside the model.
p-tehdit-modeli-sec-title: The extension bridge is part of the model
p-tehdit-modeli-sec-label: How the browser extension talks to the vault
p-tehdit-modeli-sec-body: The native messaging bridge binds only to local loopback TCP (127.0.0.1, port range 49155–49165), authenticates with a 256-bit CSPRNG pairing token stored in an OS-protected file, and then encrypts every frame with XChaCha20-Poly1305 under a session key derived with HKDF-SHA256. Cached credentials carry a five-minute lease and are zeroized on expiry; broad queries return sanitized metadata so a single message cannot bulk-exfiltrate the vault. Malware with your OS privileges can still read the token file — that residual risk is documented, not denied.
p-tehdit-modeli-tech1-desc: Vault session state is a zeroized Uint8Array in process memory. Safer than sessionStorage, but not an OS secret enclave — setup and unlock input still crosses the UI boundary.
p-tehdit-modeli-tech2-desc: Windows builds request WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE and Android sets FLAG_SECURE. This reduces ordinary screenshots and task-switcher previews; it does not stop privileged capture software.
p-tehdit-modeli-tech3-desc: Every extension bridge frame carries a fresh 24-byte nonce; unauthenticated or version-mismatched frames terminate the connection immediately.
p-tehdit-modeli-faq1-q: Can antivirus software detect my vault contents?
p-tehdit-modeli-faq1-a: No. The vault file and backups are ciphertext on disk, and the master password never touches sessionStorage. Malware running in your own session while the vault is unlocked is a different question — that is explicitly out of scope.
p-tehdit-modeli-faq2-q: Why are some attacks left out of scope?
p-tehdit-modeli-faq2-a: Because no local application can win them. Claiming protection from keyloggers or a compromised OS would be false comfort. Writing the boundary down lets you decide what KalderaShield can and cannot be responsible for.
p-tehdit-modeli-faq3-a: Yes. It is reviewed on every release, and a residual-risk register records each known gap, its status and the planned mitigation — including an accepted, documented trade-off in the extension autofill path.
p-denetim-durumu-h1: No independent audit has been completed yet
p-denetim-durumu-lead: This is the page most security software would leave unwritten. An independent third-party audit of KalderaShield has not been performed. No audit badge on this site corresponds to a completed external review, and none will appear until one exists.
p-denetim-durumu-what-title: What is verified automatically, and by whom
p-denetim-durumu-p1: What exists today is automated, reproducible verification: 2204 unit tests across 248 files, a property-based fuzz gate over import parsing, backup envelopes and attachment metadata, mutation testing with Stryker, CodeQL analysis and OpenSSF Scorecard in CI, gitleaks secret scanning, and a dependency policy that fails on any high or critical npm advisory.
p-denetim-durumu-p2: What does not exist is an external, independent expert review of the cryptographic design and implementation. Internal review reports document hundreds of findings and fixes, but they were written by the project itself. That is a different class of assurance and it is not presented as one.
p-denetim-durumu-p3: The plan is an external audit: a draft scope document already exists, listing the components in scope — cryptography, vault persistence, the extension bridge, the Tauri IPC surface — so the work can start as soon as an auditor is engaged. No date is promised before a contract exists.
p-denetim-durumu-steps-title: The verification you can do without us
p-denetim-durumu-step1-desc: The entire application is Apache-2.0 open source. The security-critical paths are documented in the threat model, and the code that implements them is on GitHub.
p-denetim-durumu-step2-desc: The test suite, fuzz gate and release-hardening scans run locally with npm and cargo commands that are documented in the repository. Nothing about the pipeline is hidden.
p-denetim-durumu-step3-desc: Every release publishes SHA-256 checksums, and the updater bundles carry minisign signatures. The verification page gives the exact commands.
p-denetim-durumu-sec-title: Why we say this on a public page
p-denetim-durumu-sec-label: Honesty is part of the design
p-denetim-durumu-sec-body: An unfinished audit marketed as an achievement is how trust products lose trust. The absence of an external audit is a real limitation: it means no independent expert has hunted for the flaw the automation misses. Stating it plainly lets you weigh the risk yourself, and gives the project a public commitment to be held to.
p-denetim-durumu-tech1-desc: 248 test files with coverage thresholds enforced at 90% lines and 80% branches; the measured baseline runs above them.
p-denetim-durumu-tech2-desc: Property-based tests throw malformed JSON, CSV, KDF parameters and backup envelopes at the importer and crypto paths on every release run.
p-denetim-durumu-tech3-desc: GitHub CodeQL analyzes the code weekly, OpenSSF Scorecard grades the supply chain, and gitleaks blocks committed secrets.
p-denetim-durumu-faq1-q: Does "no audit" mean the app is insecure?
p-denetim-durumu-faq1-a: No. It means independent experts have not validated the design. The source is open, the automated gates are strict and public, and the threat model states its limits — you can evaluate all three yourself.
p-denetim-durumu-faq2-q: When will an external audit happen?
p-denetim-durumu-faq2-a: When an auditor is engaged. The scope document is published so the engagement can start immediately; promising a date without a contract would be another claim this site refuses to make.
p-denetim-durumu-faq3-q: Will you show the audit results?
p-denetim-durumu-faq3-a: Yes. The full report, or the auditor's own publication of it, will be linked from this page, including findings that are not yet fixed.
p-dogrulama-h1: Trust the file you installed, not the page it came from
p-dogrulama-lead: Every KalderaShield release publishes SHA-256 checksums and updater signatures. Verifying takes one command. It is the difference between running a file that someone mirrored with modifications and running the file the pipeline built.
p-dogrulama-p1: SHA-256 checksums: every release ships a SHA256SUMS.txt next to the installers. The hash is computed by the release pipeline from the exact files it collected, and the collection step refuses artifacts that are not from the current build — a half-failed build cannot silently reuse an old installer.
p-dogrulama-p2: Updater signatures: the Tauri updater bundles are signed with minisign, and the public key is embedded in the application itself. If an updater offer is not correctly signed, the app refuses it.
p-dogrulama-p3: Release signatures: the tag-gated release pipeline signs every published artifact with cosign in keyless Sigstore mode, bound to the workflow run's OIDC identity. The pipeline also enforces a signing gate: Windows and macOS releases are blocked from publishing unless their artifacts are verified as signed.
p-dogrulama-p4: One honest caveat: while no code-signing certificate exists, Windows installers you build or download from CI are unsigned by Authenticode. The signing gate keeps them out of public releases; if you obtain one through a build, verify the SHA-256 hash before running it.
p-dogrulama-steps-title: How to verify in three steps
p-dogrulama-step1-title: Compute the hash of your file
p-dogrulama-step1-desc: On Windows, run Get-FileHash in PowerShell. On Linux and macOS, run sha256sum or shasum -a 256. Compare the output with the matching line in SHA256SUMS.txt.
p-dogrulama-step2-desc: Checksums are published with the release they describe. If you download SHA256SUMS.txt from the official release and your installer's hash matches it, the file is the one the pipeline produced.
p-dogrulama-step3-desc: In-app updates are checked against the minisign public key compiled into the application. You never need to trust a downloaded update file manually.
p-dogrulama-sec-label: Expected, until a signing certificate exists
p-dogrulama-sec-body: An unsigned executable with no download reputation is exactly the shape of file that Windows SmartScreen and antivirus heuristics warn about — this is a cost of having no certificate, not evidence of malware. Verify the SHA-256 hash, and if your antivirus still flags a hash that matches the published checksum, report the false positive to its vendor. The build workflow comments in the repository document this limitation openly.
p-dogrulama-tech1-desc: Published per artifact in SHA256SUMS.txt; the collector rejects installers older than the recorded build timestamp.
p-dogrulama-tech2-desc: Updater bundles are signed at build time; the verification key ships inside the app and latest.json points to the signature.
p-dogrulama-tech3-desc: Published release artifacts are signed keylessly through Sigstore, bound to the GitHub Actions OIDC identity of the release run.
p-dogrulama-faq1-q: Windows says "Windows protected your PC". What do I do?
p-dogrulama-faq1-a: That is SmartScreen reacting to an unsigned file, not a virus report. Verify the SHA-256 hash against SHA256SUMS.txt. If it matches, the file is the pipeline's output; the warning disappears permanently once releases carry a signing certificate.
p-dogrulama-faq2-a: Next to the installers in every release, and on the download page's verification section. A checksum that arrives only through a chat message is not verification — use the published one.
p-dogrulama-faq3-q: Can I verify without trusting any downloaded file?
p-dogrulama-faq3-a: Build from source: the repository builds reproducibly with documented npm and cargo commands, and the local release script produces the same artifact naming with its own checksums.
p-windows-lead: Windows 10 and 11 on x64 are supported with three install shapes: a standard NSIS setup wizard, an MSI package for managed deployment, and a portable executable that runs without installation.
p-windows-p1: The setup.exe wizard installs per-user or per-machine, adds Start-menu shortcuts and its own uninstaller. The MSI package exists for environments where software deployment expects that format. The portable executable needs none of that: unpack it and run.
p-windows-p2: All three build the same application. The vault file, encrypted backups and settings are portable between them, and the SHA-256 checksums are published for every artifact so you can verify the exact file you install.
p-windows-p3: Windows-specific protections are active: windows are requested with WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE, which keeps the app out of ordinary screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview, and Windows Hello wraps the convenience-unlock payload with a TPM 2.0-backed platform authenticator.
p-windows-step1-desc: Fetch the installer from the download page, then compare its SHA-256 hash with the matching line in SHA256SUMS.txt before running it.
p-windows-step2-desc: Choose a master password — Argon2id with 64 MiB, 4 iterations and 2 lanes stretches it into the vault key — and store the 24-word BIP-39 recovery key somewhere outside the app.
p-windows-step3-desc: Enroll platform unlock so daily access is a glance or a PIN, backed by TPM 2.0. The master password always remains the real root of the vault.
p-windows-sec-body: Windows installers do not carry an Authenticode signature yet: the project has no code-signing certificate, and its release gate blocks unsigned artifacts from being published as official releases. Until that changes, Windows SmartScreen may show "Windows protected your PC" for files you obtain from a build — verify the SHA-256 hash against the published checksums, and see the verification page for what that warning does and does not mean.
p-windows-tech1-desc: One download serves both. The application ships as a Tauri desktop app with a WebView-based front end.
p-windows-tech2-desc: The WebAuthn PRF platform authenticator wraps the unlock payload; the wrapping key material never leaves secure hardware.
p-windows-tech3-desc: App windows are excluded from ordinary screen capture. Privileged capture software is outside the threat model, as everywhere.
p-windows-faq1-q: Setup.exe, MSI or portable — which should I pick?
p-windows-faq1-a: For a personal machine, the setup wizard. For managed deployment, the MSI. For a USB stick or a machine where you prefer no installation, the portable executable.
p-windows-faq2-q: Why does SmartScreen warn about the installer?
p-windows-faq2-a: Because it is unsigned and has no download reputation. Verify the SHA-256 hash against SHA256SUMS.txt; the verification page explains the full picture, including why this disappears once a signing certificate is in place.
p-windows-faq3-q: Can I move my vault to another Windows PC?
p-windows-faq3-a: Yes. Export an encrypted .ks backup, move it, and restore it with the master password. The vault file is portable, not tied to one machine or one install shape.
p-linux-lead: Linux x64 ships in two shapes: a .deb package for Debian, Ubuntu and their derivatives, and an AppImage that runs on almost any distribution without installation.
p-linux-p1: The .deb package installs through dpkg or your distribution's software center, lands in the applications menu and can be removed through the normal package tools. The AppImage is one executable file: chmod +x and run, nothing else touched on the system.
p-linux-p2: Both carry the same application and the same security design: per-record AES-256-GCM encryption, Argon2id key derivation and the air-gap network policy. Vault files and encrypted backups move freely between the two and between Linux machines.
p-linux-p3: The Linux build uses the GTK3/WebKitGTK windowing stack that Tauri targets. That stack currently carries upstream unmaintained-binding advisories (documented in the dependency advisory register with the acceptance rationale) — they are ecosystem maintenance risks, not known exploitable paths in KalderaShield code.
p-linux-step1-desc: Fetch the .deb or AppImage from the download page and compare its SHA-256 hash with SHA256SUMS.txt before installing or running it.
p-linux-step2-desc: Choose the master password and store the 24-word BIP-39 recovery key outside the application. Argon2id parameters are recorded in the vault itself.
p-linux-step3-desc: The Chromium and Firefox extension builds live next to the desktop artifacts. Desktop pairing runs over a loopback-only IPC bridge with a pairing token.
p-linux-sec-body: Linux has no mandatory Authenticode-style signing, so verification is hash-based: always check the SHA-256 checksums published with the release. The updater bundles are minisign-signed regardless. The dependency advisory register lists every accepted advisory with its reason, and accepts none that is reachable from the vault, crypto or IPC trust boundaries.
p-linux-tech1-desc: Installs with dpkg/apt and integrates with the applications menu; removed with the package manager like any other software.
p-linux-tech2-desc: A single executable for almost any x64 distribution. No root, no install step, deletable like a document.
p-linux-tech3-desc: The upstream Tauri default on Linux. Its unmaintained GTK3-binding advisories are documented and accepted with rationale, re-evaluated on every Tauri update.
p-linux-faq1-q: AppImage or .deb — which should I use?
p-linux-faq1-a: Use .deb on Debian, Ubuntu, Mint and derivatives for menu integration and clean removal. Use the AppImage anywhere else, or when you want a zero-footprint install.
p-linux-faq2-q: Does the Linux version have every desktop feature?
p-linux-faq2-a: Yes, minus platform-specific conveniences that have no Linux equivalent, such as Windows Hello or Touch ID. Hardware-wrapped unlock is available through PRF-capable FIDO2 security keys instead.
p-linux-faq3-q: Can I use the same vault on Linux and Windows?
p-linux-faq3-a: Yes. Encrypted backups are portable across all desktop platforms. Create the backup on one machine and restore it with the master password on the other.
p-macos-lead: macOS ships as a universal build: one .dmg that installs on Apple Silicon and Intel Macs, built on macOS itself as the platform requires.
p-macos-p1: The .dmg contains a universal application: it runs natively on Apple Silicon and Intel without Rosetta. The bundle is built on macOS, because macOS packages cannot be produced correctly on other platforms.
p-macos-p2: macOS-specific protections are active: Touch ID wraps the convenience-unlock payload with a Secure Enclave-backed WebAuthn PRF platform authenticator, and PRF-capable FIDO2 security keys such as a YubiKey 5 can serve as the wrapping authenticator instead.
p-macos-p3: Everything else is the same design as every other platform: per-record AES-256-GCM encryption, Argon2id with 64 MiB / 4 iterations / 2 lanes, the air-gap network policy and portable encrypted backups.
p-macos-step1-desc: Fetch the .dmg from the download page and compare its SHA-256 hash with SHA256SUMS.txt before mounting it.
p-macos-step2-desc: Choose the master password and store the 24-word BIP-39 recovery key outside the application, in a place you control.
p-macos-step3-desc: Enroll platform unlock so daily access is a fingerprint, backed by the Secure Enclave. The master password remains the root of the vault and the only full recovery path.
p-macos-sec-body: The application does not carry a Developer ID signature yet, and it is not notarized: the release pipeline blocks macOS artifacts from public release until real Developer ID signing is configured. Until then, a build you obtain outside the pipeline is subject to Gatekeeper's unsigned-application checks — verify the SHA-256 hash against the published checksums, and right-click → Open is the local override for a file you have verified yourself.
p-macos-tech1-desc: One .dmg serves both architectures natively. Built on macOS, as the platform's own packaging rules require.
p-macos-tech2-desc: The PRF-derived wrapping key never leaves the secure hardware. Re-enrollment or device replacement degrades convenience only, never vault access.
p-macos-tech3-desc: PRF-capable security keys (YubiKey 5, firmware 5.3+) can wrap the unlock payload; unlocking then requires the physical key.
p-macos-faq1-q: Does the universal build run on both M-series and Intel Macs?
p-macos-faq1-a: Yes. The application is compiled for both architectures and macOS picks the right slice automatically. No Rosetta translation is involved.
p-macos-faq2-q: Why does macOS warn about the application?
p-macos-faq2-a: Because it is not signed with a Developer ID certificate or notarized yet. Verify the SHA-256 hash against the published checksums first; the verification page explains the whole story.
p-macos-faq3-q: If I lose my Mac, do I lose my vault?
p-macos-faq3-a: No. The vault file is never hardware-sealed. Restore an encrypted backup on any other device with the master password — Touch ID wraps convenience, not access.
p-android-lead: Android 7.0 (API 24) and newer are supported with a signed release APK: the same local-first vault, with hardware-backed biometric unlock and Android screen-capture protection.
p-android-p1: The Android app is a full KalderaShield: all five record types, folders, tags, search, encrypted backups and attachments. Release builds are signed, built with R8 shrinking and verified by release-hardening scans that check for debuggable flags, backup exposure and cleartext traffic.
p-android-p2: Biometric unlock is hardware-bound: the wrapping key lives in AndroidKeyStore as an auth-bound, non-exportable key that is invalidated when biometric enrollment changes. Unlock goes through BiometricPrompt with a CryptoObject, so the OS auth token is bound to the key's crypto operation.
p-android-p3: Android sets FLAG_SECURE on the main activity, keeping the app out of screenshots, screen recordings and the recents preview. Import and export go through the system document picker, so every read and write location is one you explicitly chose.
p-android-step1-desc: Enable installation from your chosen file source, install the APK and verify its SHA-256 hash against the published checksums.
p-android-step2-desc: The same Argon2id parameters as desktop — 64 MiB, 4 iterations, 2 lanes — and the same 24-word BIP-39 recovery key to store safely.
p-android-step3-desc: Use BiometricPrompt to wrap daily access with the device's secure hardware. The master password remains the only root of the vault.
p-android-sec-body: Android biometric behaviour varies across OEM builds. The public release gating therefore requires explicit device-matrix evidence (Pixel, Samsung, Xiaomi, Android 12–15) before production biometric claims are made, and this page makes none beyond what the platform contract guarantees. The Android Credential Provider passkey filling remains outside the current release boundary.
p-android-tech1-desc: Auth-bound, non-exportable key with setUserAuthenticationRequired; invalidated automatically when biometrics are re-enrolled.
p-android-tech2-desc: The main activity is excluded from screenshots, screen recording and the recents preview by the OS.
p-android-tech3-desc: Import, export and download flows use the system picker bridge; the app never gains broad storage permissions.
p-android-faq1-a: Android 7.0 (API 24) and newer, targeted at API 35. Devices without a biometric sensor still work with the master password alone.
p-android-faq2-q: What happens if I change my fingerprint?
p-android-faq2-a: The AndroidKeyStore wrapping key is invalidated by design when biometric enrollment changes. You unlock with the master password and re-enroll platform unlock — vault access is never affected.
p-android-faq3-q: Can I share the vault with my desktop?
p-android-faq3-a: Yes. Export an encrypted .ks backup through the document picker, move it however you like, and restore it on the desktop with the master password.
p-eklenti-h1: Filling passwords is the riskiest moment. We designed for it.
p-eklenti-lead: The KalderaShield extension is a Manifest V3 companion for Chromium and Firefox. It fills credentials only on sites it can bind to an existing record, talks to the desktop app over an encrypted loopback bridge, and collects nothing.
p-eklenti-what-title: Autofill with a bouncer at the door
p-eklenti-p1: The extension injects a content script into http/https pages and offers to fill credentials for the site you are on. Domain matching is validated down to eTLD+1 — lookalike domains on different registrable domains do not receive another site's credentials, and a phishing-alert latch keeps warning once a mismatch is detected.
p-eklenti-p2: It has no broad page powers: the manifest requests nativeMessaging, activeTab and storage, the extension pages' CSP is script-src 'self', and the Firefox build declares data_collection_permissions: none. There is no analytics SDK and no telemetry in the bundle.
p-eklenti-p3: The pairing dialog on the desktop side must be accepted before the bridge works at all, credentials are leased to the bridge for five minutes at a time and zeroized on expiry, and a revoke action wipes the lease and rotates the pairing token immediately.
p-eklenti-step1-title: The site asks, the extension checks
p-eklenti-step1-desc: The content script finds a login form on the page you are on and asks the background worker. The worker validates the tab URL against the records it may offer — same eTLD+1 or an explicitly saved match.
p-eklenti-step2-desc: The request travels over the native messaging bridge to the desktop app, which returns only credentials bound to that site — broad queries return sanitized metadata with empty passwords.
p-eklenti-step3-title: The fill is bound to the tab
p-eklenti-step3-desc: Filling is gated by tab-URL validation on the return path. The extension never accepts fill requests from web pages directly: pages cannot reach the extension's channel at all.
p-eklenti-sec-title: What the extension does not do
p-eklenti-sec-body: The extension stores no vault: it is a window into the desktop app, and without the paired desktop running it has nothing to give. It does not sync anything to any server, it does not read pages you have not activated it on, and malware with your OS privileges could reach the pairing token file — a residual risk documented in the threat model rather than denied.
p-eklenti-tech1-desc: nativeMessaging, activeTab, storage. No broad host access, no scripts evaluated from remote sources, CSP locked to 'self'.
p-eklenti-tech2-desc: Native messaging talks to the desktop over loopback TCP only; every frame is XChaCha20-Poly1305-encrypted under an HKDF-derived session key.
p-eklenti-tech3-desc: The Firefox build ships as a Mozilla-signed XPI (AMO), so it installs persistently on Release and Beta; the Chromium build loads unpacked or through your organization's policy.
p-eklenti-faq1-q: Can the extension work without the desktop app?
p-eklenti-faq1-a: No, by design. It holds no vault copy, so a stolen laptop with the extension installed still holds nothing. Everything it can offer comes live from the paired, locked-or-unlocked desktop session.
p-eklenti-faq2-q: What stops a fake website from getting my credentials?
p-eklenti-faq2-a: Domain validation at eTLD+1, a phishing-alert latch, and the fact that fill offers are bound to validated tab URLs. A different registrable domain is a different site, whatever it looks like.
p-eklenti-faq3-q: Does the extension see what I type on every page?
p-eklenti-faq3-a: No. The content script is active on http/https pages, but it only reacts to login forms and to your explicit requests through the popup or keyboard. There is no keystroke logging.
p-kaynak-kodu-h1: The whole thing is on GitHub
p-kaynak-kodu-lead: KalderaShield is Apache-2.0 licensed open source: the desktop app, the Android app, the browser extension, the native messaging host and this site. Every security claim on this website can be traced to code or to a test that runs in public CI.
p-kaynak-kodu-p1: The desktop application pairs a React and TypeScript front end with a Rust core through Tauri 2: the UI renders in the system WebView, the native side handles the updater, the extension bridge and platform integrations. Vault persistence runs on wa-sqlite with a versioned schema envelope.
p-kaynak-kodu-p2: The browser extension is a Manifest V3 TypeScript build for Chromium and Firefox, and the Android app is a Tauri Android project with AndroidKeyStore biometric binding. The native messaging host and the IPC bridge live in the Rust workspace, where the pairing token, lease and frame-encryption logic are easiest to audit.
p-kaynak-kodu-p3: The site itself is plain committed HTML — no build step for deployment — with generator scripts and quality gates checked in next to the pages they produce.
p-kaynak-kodu-step1-desc: 248 test files with enforced coverage thresholds: 90% lines, 90% statements, 85% functions, 80% branches. A regression below the threshold fails the build, not a dashboard.
p-kaynak-kodu-step2-desc: fast-check property tests hammer importer, backup and attachment paths with malformed input. Stryker mutation testing grades test quality. Dedicated gates check CSP hardening, release artifacts, debug markers and secrets.
p-kaynak-kodu-step3-desc: CodeQL analyzes the code, OpenSSF Scorecard grades the repository posture, gitleaks blocks committed secrets, and the dependency policy fails on any high or critical advisory with documented acceptance for the rest.
p-kaynak-kodu-sec-title: What open source here means — and does not
p-kaynak-kodu-sec-body: Open source lets anyone read the code; it does not by itself prove that anyone has. Reading is the whole point: the threat model, the acceptance registers and the audit scope are in the repository so reviewers start from the same map. An independent audit has not been completed — the audit status page says so directly.
p-kaynak-kodu-tech1-desc: React UI, extension and shared vault logic, strictly typed; no React inline styles, enforced by the CSP gate.
p-kaynak-kodu-tech2-desc: Tauri 2 commands, native messaging host, loopback IPC bridge and updater plumbing; cargo fmt and focused atomic-write tests gate every release.
p-kaynak-kodu-tech3-desc: The whole project plus a THIRD-PARTY license file for bundled components. No proprietary blobs in the installers.
p-kaynak-kodu-faq1-q: How do I report a security vulnerability?
p-kaynak-kodu-faq1-a: Privately, never as a public issue: GitHub private vulnerability reporting or the email in SECURITY.md. Acknowledgement within 48 hours, triage within 7 days, coordinated disclosure within 90.
p-kaynak-kodu-faq2-a: Yes — through GitHub pull requests. The gates described above run on every change, so the fastest way to help is a change that keeps them green and includes its own tests.
p-kaynak-kodu-faq3-q: Can I build the installers myself?
p-kaynak-kodu-faq3-a: Yes. The local release guide documents the exact commands per platform, and the release script collects artifacts with SHA-256 checksums into release-local/<platform>/.
p-sss-lead: Short answers, no marketing layer. Every answer that makes a claim links to the page that backs it.
p-sss-p1: KalderaShield is a free, open-source password manager under the Apache-2.0 license. There is no paid tier, no subscription and no premium version — the roadmap deliberately contains none, and a pricing page would be misleading for a product with no price.
p-sss-p2: It is local-first: your vault is stored encrypted on your device, there is no KalderaShield account and no server-side copy of your data. Optional sync through your own WebDAV or S3 storage uploads only the encrypted payload.
p-sss-p3: It runs on Windows, Linux and macOS desktops, on Android, and as a browser extension for Chromium and Firefox that fills credentials from the paired desktop app.
p-sss-step1-title: Choose a master password you can remember
p-sss-step1-desc: Argon2id stretches it into the vault key, but no parameter change can recover a password you did not store. The 24-word recovery key is the second path — save it outside the app.
p-sss-step2-title: Make an encrypted backup on day one
p-sss-step2-desc: The .ks backup is encrypted with your backup password and restorable on any platform. Keep one copy outside the device.
p-sss-step3-desc: Compare the installer's SHA-256 hash with the published checksums. One command, and you know you are running the pipeline's output.
p-sss-sec-title: What KalderaShield deliberately does not do
p-sss-sec-body: No cloud sync between KalderaShield servers. No account system, no email-based password reset. No recovery of a lost master password — nobody, including us, can re-derive it. No protection against malware running in your own OS session while the vault is unlocked. No pricing page, because there is nothing to buy. Each of these is a design decision documented in the threat model or the plan, not a missing feature.
p-sss-tech1-desc: CSV and JSON import normalizes data from common managers before saving; the fuzz gate hammers the importer with malformed files on every release run.
p-sss-tech2-desc: The .ks format uses Argon2id and AES-256-GCM. Backups restore on Windows, Linux, macOS and Android alike.
p-sss-tech3-desc: The air-gap policy blocks unexpected outbound traffic; the extension declares data collection of none. There is nothing to opt out of.
p-sss-faq1-a: Yes, under the Apache-2.0 license. No subscription, no premium tier, no feature locked behind payment.
p-sss-faq2-a: No. There is no account and no server-side vault. You create a local vault protected by a master password, optionally wrapped by your device's biometrics.
p-sss-faq3-q: What happens if I forget my master password?
p-sss-faq3-a: Unlock with the 24-word BIP-39 recovery key, or restore an encrypted backup. Without one of those, the data cannot be recovered — by you, by the app, or by anyone else.
p-sss-faq4-q: Can I import from 1Password, Bitwarden or LastPass?
p-sss-faq4-a: Yes, through CSV and JSON export files. The importer normalizes the common formats before saving, and malformed input is handled by a fuzz-tested parser rather than trusted.
p-sss-faq5-q: How do I move my vault to a new device?
p-sss-faq5-a: Export an encrypted .ks backup, transfer the file yourself, and restore it with the master password on any platform. The vault is portable by design.
p-sss-faq6-q: Is my data synced between devices?
p-sss-faq6-a: Not automatically. There is no KalderaShield cloud. Optional sync uploads only the encrypted payload to WebDAV or S3 storage that you configure and own.
p-sss-faq7-q: Can the browser extension leak my passwords?
p-sss-faq7-a: The extension stores no vault — it holds nothing when the desktop app is absent. Fills are bound to validated tab URLs at eTLD+1, bridge frames are encrypted, and broad credential queries return sanitized metadata. The residual risks are documented in the threat model.
p-sss-faq8-a: No independent audit has been completed yet — the audit status page states this openly along with the automated verification that exists. Claiming otherwise would be easy; auditing is how it gets fixed.

final-cta-title: Take Back Control of Your Passwords
final-cta-desc: Free, open source, serverless. Download, verify and keep your vault on your device.
how-title: Four steps from a master password to an encrypted vault
how-desc: Nothing on this page contacts a server. Every step runs on the device you are reading it on.
how-step1-desc: It never leaves this device in any form, and there is no reset link, because there is no account to reset.
how-step2-desc: The password is stretched into a key with Argon2id, then HKDF-SHA256 splits it into an isolated key for each record.
how-step3-title: Every record is sealed with AES-256-GCM
how-step3-desc: The vault file on disk holds ciphertext and its authentication tag. Reading one without the key fails rather than returning a wrong value.
how-step4-desc: Biometrics, a security key or the 24-word recovery kit release the key again on this device. No network request is involved.
dl-cli-note: The script fetches the version number and the SHA-256 digests from GitHub Releases while it runs, compares them against SHA256SUMS.txt, and stops the installation if anything does not match.
dl-android-desc: Hardware-backed Keystore and Biometric API integration.
d404-title: The page you asked for has moved, or never existed.
d404-desc: It may be a mistyped link, or the page may have been renamed. These are the ways back.
